title: MLE of the Mean Vector and Covariance Matrix
breadcrumb: Module 8 · Multivariate Analysis · MLE of mean vector and covariance
objectives: Obtain the mean vector MLE as the sample mean vector.
Obtain the covariance MLE using divisor n.
Distinguish the MLE from unbiased sample covariance using n−1.
Compute both estimators and recognise rank constraints.

prereq.name: Multivariate normal distribution
prereq.why: The likelihood is built from the multivariate normal density.

prereq.name: Matrix transpose and determinant
prereq.why: The log-likelihood contains a determinant and quadratic form.

prereq.name: Sample mean and covariance
prereq.why: The estimators use centred outer products.

traps: The covariance MLE divides by n, not n−1.
The unbiased sample covariance divides by n−1; it is not the MLE.
When μ is unknown, centre observations at x̄, not zero.
Use outer products to retain cross-products.
The estimate is symmetric positive semidefinite.
The centred covariance rank is at most min(p,n−1); if n≤p it is singular.

sheet: For iid Nₚ(μ,Σ), log L=−np/2 log(2π)−n/2 log|Σ|−(1/2)Σᵢ(xᵢ−μ)′Σ⁻¹(xᵢ−μ).
Each outer product is p×p; the estimate is symmetric positive semidefinite.
rank(Σ̂)≤min(p,n−1); if n≤p, it is singular.
tricks: Compute the centred outer-product sum once and divide at the end.
shortcuts: Check x̄ has p coordinates and Σ̂ is p×p.
Check symmetry and nonnegative diagonal entries.
For n=3, the MLE is two-thirds of the unbiased covariance.
remember: Mean vector MLE is the sample mean vector.
Covariance MLE uses n; unbiased covariance uses n−1.

howto: Find x̄ first. Subtract it from every observation. Form each deviation outer product, add the matrices, and divide by n for the Gaussian covariance MLE. Divide by n−1 only when asked for unbiased sample covariance.

scenes.title: Vectors, covariance and outer products
body: A multivariate observation is a p×1 column vector. A sample of n subjects gives n such vectors.
The mean vector contains one sample mean per variable. A covariance matrix has variances on its diagonal and covariances off the diagonal; it is symmetric.
For d=xᵢ−x̄, the outer product dd′ is p×p. Adding these matrices gives the centred sum-of-products matrix.

items.ask: If x is p×1, what are dimensions of xx′?
refresh: A p×1 column vector has p rows and one column. Its transpose has one row and p columns, so xx′ is a p×p matrix. This is the outer product, not the scalar inner product x′x. The dimensions matter because a covariance matrix must have one row and one column for every measured variable.

The (j,k) entry of xx′ is xⱼxₖ. Swapping j and k leaves the product unchanged, so the outer-product matrix is symmetric. For any vector a, a′xx′a=(x′a)², which cannot be negative; therefore each outer product is positive semidefinite.

items.ask: What does the covariance matrix diagonal contain?
refresh: The jth diagonal entry of a covariance matrix is Var(Xⱼ), the variance of variable j. It describes how widely that variable varies around its population mean. Diagonal entries are nonnegative, and they are positive when the corresponding variable is non-degenerate.

The off-diagonal entry in position (j,k) is Cov(Xⱼ,Xₖ), which describes how the two variables vary together. Covariance matrices are symmetric because Cov(Xⱼ,Xₖ)=Cov(Xₖ,Xⱼ); hence entry (j,k) equals entry (k,j).

items.ask: What is the sample mean vector?
refresh: The sample mean vector is formed by averaging each coordinate across the n observations. If every observation is p×1, the resulting mean vector is also p×1. Its jth entry is the ordinary sample mean of the jth variable.

For a multivariate normal sample, maximising the likelihood with respect to the unknown mean vector gives μ̂=x̄. This estimate is then used to centre every observation before the covariance matrix MLE is calculated.

scenes.title: What does the likelihood fit?
body: For independent observations from Nₚ(μ,Σ), the likelihood rewards parameter values that make the observed vectors plausible.
The mean estimate locates the centre of the cloud. The covariance estimate describes spread, orientation and linear dependence.
The normal covariance MLE averages centred outer products over n observations. The unbiased covariance uses n−1 because estimating the mean consumes one degree of freedom.

scenario.title: Estimating a bivariate cloud
body: A researcher records two measurements for each of three subjects. The sample mean gives the centre. Each subject's deviation is a two-coordinate vector; its outer product records squared deviations and their cross-product. Summing these matrices estimates scatter around the fitted centre. For maximum likelihood under the normal model, average over all three observations, so divide by three. The unbiased sample covariance instead divides by two.
scenario.q: What distinguishes the two covariance estimates?
scenario.answer: The MLE divides by n; the unbiased estimator divides by n−1.

ask.q: Why does maximum likelihood use n rather than n−1?
ask.nudge: Unbiasedness is a different criterion from likelihood maximisation.

blocks.body: X₁,…,Xₙ are independent Nₚ(μ,Σ), where μ is p×1 and Σ is symmetric positive definite.
Maximise first over μ to obtain x̄. Substitute it and maximise over Σ; the result is the centred outer-product sum divided by n.

nodes.label: Sum outer products; divide by n

ask.q: Which term contains the determinant of Σ?
ask.nudge: It is the log-determinant penalty in the log-likelihood.

scenes.problem: The centred outer-product sum is M=[[12,6],[6,8]] from n=4 observations.

steps.say: For the MLE, divide by n.
steps.why: The normal likelihood averages over all observations.

steps.say: For unbiased covariance, divide by n−1.
steps.why: Estimating the mean uses one degree of freedom.
Divide the centred sum entry by n.

scenes.after: The MLE is M/4; the unbiased covariance is M/3. The top-left MLE entry is 3.

ask.q: Which estimate is larger entry by entry here?
ask.nudge: The same positive matrix is divided by three versus four.

blocks.body: Σ̂_MLE=((n−1)/n)S. The MLE is biased downward for Σ; S is unbiased under iid sampling.
The centred deviations sum to zero, leaving n−1 degrees of freedom after estimating the mean.
rank(Σ̂)≤min(p,n−1). When n≤p, the centred sample covariance is singular.
The estimate is symmetric and positive semidefinite. It is positive definite only if centred observations span the full p-dimensional space.

ask.q: If n=5, what is the ratio Σ̂_MLE/S?
ask.nudge: Compare denominators while keeping the same centred sum.

scenario.title: Two measurements from three units
body: A pilot study records response and time scores (0,1), (2,1) and (1,4). Their centre is (1,2). After centring, cross-products from the first two participants cancel, so estimated covariance is zero although both variables vary. The covariance MLE divides the centred outer-product sum by three. The result is diagonal with entries two-thirds and two. This illustrates why the off-diagonal estimate depends on signs and magnitudes of paired deviations, not just separate variances.
scenario.q: Why is the estimated covariance off-diagonal zero?
scenario.answer: Positive and negative cross-products cancel in the sum.

ask.q: What quick checks can you make on your final matrix?
ask.nudge: Check symmetry and nonnegative diagonal entries.

scenes.title: Exam traps: denominator and centring
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false.

items.claim: The normal covariance MLE with unknown mean divides by n−1.
items.why: The MLE divides by n; n−1 gives unbiased sample covariance.

items.claim: The MLE of μ is the sample mean vector.
items.why: Differentiating the log-likelihood with respect to μ gives x̄.

items.claim: The covariance MLE uses centred outer products.
items.why: Each term is (xᵢ−x̄)(xᵢ−x̄)′ and retains cross-products.

items.claim: If n≤p, the centred sample covariance must be full rank.
items.why: Its rank is at most n−1, below p when n≤p.

ask.q: Which word in a question signals use of n−1?

scenes.check: The MLE is 5/6 of S, so its diagonal entries are smaller.

solution.why: Both estimators use the same centred sum.

scenes.title: Exam routine: centre, outer-product, divide
body: For iid Nₚ(μ,Σ), the mean MLE is μ̂=x̄.
The covariance MLE is the centred outer-product sum divided by n.
The unbiased sample covariance uses the same sum divided by n−1.
Σ̂_MLE=((n−1)/n)S. Centre at x̄ when μ is unknown.
